newsitem.title: UK: Treasuries dip in London, await second data leg.
newsitem.headline: Treasuries dip in London, await second data leg.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries dipped on profit-taking in London on Wednesday, heartened by Tuesday's data but unwilling to push their luck before the next set of numbers, analysts said.
"There's been a bit of selling in the long end out of Asia," said a trader at a French bank in London. "Some Asian accounts have been hanging around until we come in -- 30-year, 10-year stuff."
At 0927 GMT, the long bond was quoted at 95-09, yielding 7.00 percent, compared with 95-11 in Tokyo and 95-16 and the close in New York on Tuesday.

The market posted one of its best sessions since last year on Tuesday after a string of softer than expected data weakened market expectations of an interest rate rise when the Federal Reserve meets on May 20.

The first quarter employment cost index rose 0.6 percent against expectations of a 0.9 percent rise, March durable goods orders fell 3.0 percent versus forecasts for a flat figure and April consumer confidence came in at 116.8 compared with 118.5 in March.
But with preliminary first quarter growth data and regional purchasing manager reports due this session, the market was taking little for granted.

"Although it has (the ECI) scared a few people into thinking they're not going to go and taken some people out of flattening trades, I don't know if people would want to be long the front end at this point in time," the trader at the French bank said.
He still expected the Fed to raise rates, perhaps at its next policy meeting.
"What I'm hearing is, this is the opportunity to put on shorts, if not put options while the volatility is so low," he said.
Adam Chester, bond strategist at Yamaichi International here, expected the Fed to move in May as GDP data would come out strong.
"All the activity numbers we've had over the last three months indicate we are going to get a strong GDP number of around 4.0 percent which is pretty much in line with the consensus," Chester said.
He said the market could get a lift if the implicit deflator section of the data -- the broadest measure of U.S. inflation -- continued to remain restrained even if growth continued robust.
The deflator was expected to come in at 1.7 percent, according to a Reuters survey.
June T-bond futures were at 108-27 in automated trade, down three ticks from Tuesday's Chicago settlement. --Jacqueline Thorpe, International Bonds Unit +44 171 542 6176
